paper.title: QPUs Are Not GPUs: Why Quantum Processors Need Constant Classical Control

questions.theme: Where QPUs fit in scientific computing
questions.prompt: Where does the paper see the strongest case for quantum computing in science?

choices.text: Simulating quantum systems themselves, such as molecules, materials, and catalysts
Combinatorial optimization at practical problem sizes
Solving large linear systems for typical scientific workloads
Climate and weather modeling

questions.explanation: Using a quantum device to model a quantum system has the clearest theoretical grounding, though advantage has not yet been shown on physically relevant problems. The paper calls optimization contested and quantum linear algebra narrow.
questions.quote: The strongest case is simulating quantum systems themselves: the electronic structure of molecules and materials, catalysts and battery chemistry, and strongly correlated physical systems
questions.location: 2 Where Quantum Processors Fit in Scientific Computing (p. 2)

questions.theme: Workloads where QPUs are not a consideration
questions.prompt: For which of these workloads does the paper say QPUs are not a practical consideration on any planning horizon visible today? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Computational fluid dynamics
Electronic structure of molecules and materials
Climate and weather modeling
Structural mechanics
Quantum dynamics and condensed-matter physics

questions.explanation: Most of today's scientific computing portfolio is outside the reach of QPUs, and classical CPUs and GPUs remain the right tools. Electronic structure and quantum dynamics are the paper's strong candidates.
questions.quote: For most of today's scientific computing portfolio, including computational fluid dynamics, climate and weather modeling, structural mechanics, and classical molecular dynamics, QPUs are not a practical consideration on any planning horizon visible today.
questions.location: 2 Where Quantum Processors Fit in Scientific Computing (p. 2)

questions.prompt: In the familiar GPU offload model, what happens if the host is slow to respond?

choices.text: The results become unreliable and must be recomputed
Running time grows exponentially as a backlog builds
The device sits idle and throughput suffers, but the results are still correct
The kernel aborts and must be relaunched

questions.explanation: Once a GPU kernel is running it needs nothing further from the host to produce a correct answer, which is why the paper compares a GPU to an inherently stable airliner. Exponential slowdown from a backlog is the QPU failure mode.
questions.quote: If the host is slow to respond, the device sits idle and throughput suffers, but the results it produces are still correct.
questions.location: 3 The Familiar Model: Accelerators as Offload Engines (p. 3)

questions.prompt: Which aircraft does the paper say a QPU most resembles?

choices.text: An unstable fighter that needs a flight control computer making continuous corrections
A stable airliner that keeps flying straight and level if the pilot lets go
A glider that needs no power once it is aloft
A drone flown entirely from a remote ground station

questions.explanation: Like a fighter designed to be unstable, a QPU cannot stay on course by itself; the classical system must keep correcting it. The stable airliner is the paper's picture of a GPU.
questions.quote: A QPU is much closer to the fighter than to the airliner.
questions.location: 4 A Device That Cannot Fly Itself (p. 3)

questions.prompt: Why does useful quantum computation require quantum error correction?

choices.text: Classical decoders introduce errors that must be removed
Measuring a qubit always destroys the whole computation
QPUs cannot be shielded from the heat of nearby GPUs
The best two-qubit operations fail roughly once in a few hundred to a thousand attempts

questions.explanation: Useful scientific computations will need billions of operations or more, far beyond what such error rates allow. Error correction closes the gap by encoding one reliable logical qubit across many physical qubits.
questions.quote: Across the leading qubit technologies, the best two-qubit operations now fail roughly once in every few hundred to a thousand attempts
questions.location: 4 A Device That Cannot Fly Itself (p. 3)

questions.prompt: What do syndrome measurements do in quantum error correction?

choices.text: They read out the final answer of the computation
They reveal errors without disturbing the encoded information
They apply corrections directly to each physical qubit
They copy the quantum state to classical memory as a backup

questions.explanation: The device repeatedly runs these checks, and a classical decoder interprets each round to infer which errors occurred and what correction to apply. Applying corrections is the job of the decoder and controller, not the measurement.
questions.quote: The device repeatedly measures a set of checks across its physical qubits, called syndrome measurements, which reveal errors without disturbing the encoded information.
questions.location: 4 A Device That Cannot Fly Itself (p. 4)

questions.prompt: What happens if the classical decoder cannot keep up with the quantum device?

choices.text: The device idles, but its results remain correct
The QPU switches to a slower, error-free mode
Unprocessed syndrome data accumulates, delays compound, and runtime can grow exponentially
The computation finishes on time but with lower precision

questions.explanation: Some logical operations cannot proceed until the decoder answers, so a backlog forces each dependent step to wait. Idling with correct results is the GPU case, which is the contrast the paper draws.
questions.quote: Because each dependent step must wait for the backlog to clear, delays compound, and runtime can grow exponentially with the number of such steps.
questions.location: 4 A Device That Cannot Fly Itself (p. 4)

questions.prompt: The classical side of a quantum system is a stack of layers on different timescales. What do the inner layers demand?

choices.text: Remote access through job submission, like other HPC resources
Only occasional host attention, as with a GPU kernel
Large shared-memory nodes in a separate data center
Deterministic, low-latency classical computing physically close to the quantum device

questions.explanation: Pulse generation, readout, and real-time decoding run on nanosecond and microsecond deadlines. Only the outermost layer resembles the accelerator model, and remote access can serve only the outer layers.
questions.quote: The inner layers demand deterministic, low-latency classical computing physically close to the quantum device.

questions.theme: A reversal in the role of GPUs
questions.prompt: What "interesting reversal" does the paper point out about GPUs?

choices.text: QPUs are likely to replace GPUs as the main accelerator in HPC nodes
GPUs may find a growing role inside the quantum control system, serving the QPU
GPU programming models already support hard real-time co-execution with QPUs
GPUs are becoming too slow to host quantum workloads

questions.explanation: The device that defined the offload model may end up working for the QPU, for example running decoders. The paper also notes that today's GPU programming models were built for handing work off, not hard real-time co-execution.
questions.quote: The device that defined the offload model may find a growing role inside the quantum control system, serving the QPU rather than the other way around.

questions.prompt: What is the paper's main conclusion for system architects and facility planners?

choices.text: A QPU can be integrated as one more accelerator in the node, with a thin driver layer
Quantum devices should be reached only remotely, away from HPC systems
Integrating quantum computing into HPC is as much a classical systems problem as a quantum one
Facilities should wait until qubit error rates fall before planning any integration

questions.explanation: The classical system around a QPU is a substantial, specialized computing system that must scale with the device. The paper explicitly rejects the thin-driver picture, which is the near-miss here.
questions.quote: What seems clear is that integrating quantum computing into HPC is as much a classical systems problem as a quantum one
